title: One Festival, Many Stories: How Four Faiths Celebrate Diwali
excerpt: Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists all light lamps at Diwali, but each faith marks a different story. Here is what each tradition commemorates, and the dates for 2026.
body:
• Diwali is observed by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists — more than a billion people in India and across the diaspora.
  • The name comes from Deepavali, "a row of lights"; the lamps symbolize the victory of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance.
  • Each faith attaches the festival to its own story: Rama's return, Mahavira's liberation, Guru Hargobind's release, and, for some Buddhists, Ashoka's conversion.
  • In 2026 the five days run November 6-11, from Dhanteras to Bhai Dooj, with the main day on Sunday, November 8.

Ask four families what Diwali commemorates and you may hear four stories. The Festival of Lights is celebrated across faiths by more than a billion people in India and the diaspora, according to the Associated Press. Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists all observe it — but each tradition lights the lamps for a different reason, and the differences are the point.

A Row of Lights

Diwali is derived from Deepavali, which means "a row of lights." Celebrants light rows of clay oil lamps, called diyas, outside their homes to symbolize the victory of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance. The festival lasts five days, and traditionally the third day is considered the most important, when families gather to light candles, eat sweets and place lit lamps in their public-facing windows, according to an Interfaith America essay by a scholar of Asian religion.

The Hindu Stories: Rama, Krishna and Lakshmi

Hindu observance holds more than one story, depending on where a family comes from. In northern India, Diwali honors the triumphant return of Lord Rama, his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana from a 14-year exile, after Rama's defeat of the demon king Ravana. Ayodhya is said to have welcomed him home with rows of lamps.

In southern India, many families commemorate a different victory: Lord Krishna's destruction of the demon Narakasura, who had imprisoned women and tormented his subjects. Other Hindu traditions associate the festival with the goddess Lakshmi, worshipped in the north as the goddess of wealth and prosperity. One tradition holds that Lakshmi emerged from the churning of the ocean of milk and chose to marry Vishnu.

The Jain Observance: Mahavira's Liberation

Jains observe Diwali as the day Lord Mahavira, the last of the great Jain teachers, attained nirvana — liberation from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. The lamps here mark an enlightenment rather than a homecoming or a battle: Mahavira, the 24th spiritual teacher of the Jain path, reached release from samsara, the repeating cycle of life and death.

The Sikh Observance: Bandi Chhor Divas

Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, a day that overlaps with Diwali, to commemorate the release of Guru Hargobind, the sixth Sikh guru, from imprisonment by the Mughal emperor Jahangir. According to the Interfaith America account, Guru Hargobind secured the release of 52 other imprisoned men alongside his own. Popular legend holds that each of the 52 held onto a thread of his cloak, so all of them walked out with him. For Sikhs, the day carries a theme of liberation — the guru's release read as an act of service and social justice as much as personal freedom.

The Buddhist Observance

Some Buddhists observe the day as the one when the emperor Ashoka, who ruled in the third century B.C., converted to Buddhism. The observance is not universal across Buddhist communities. The Associated Press frames it as the Diwali story held by Buddhists who mark the festival: the moment a ruler known for conquest turned toward the Buddha's teaching.

One Theme Across the Traditions

Why do four religions share one festival? Scholars suggest the rituals came first and the explanations followed. The Interfaith America essay notes that the multiplicity of stories may itself be the message: read together, they argue that good — whether as an avatar of Vishnu, an enlightened Jain teacher or an imprisoned guru freed with 52 others — triumphs over demons, injustice and ignorance. The Associated Press puts it more simply: every story carries the victory of good over evil.

Diwali 2026: The Dates to Know

The festival follows the Hindu lunar calendar, usually falling in late October or early November. In 2026, Dhanteras opens on Friday, November 6, followed by Naraka Chaturdashi, or Chhoti Diwali, on Saturday, November 7. The main day — Diwali itself, the night of Lakshmi Puja, on the new moon of the month of Kartik — falls on Sunday, November 8. Govardhan Puja follows on Tuesday, November 10 and Bhai Dooj on Wednesday, November 11, according to the Hindu Hub Diwali 2026 guide. For diaspora families in the United States, the Sunday main day puts the central night of the festival on a weekend this year. The stories are traced in full in the Interfaith America essay on Diwali's many stories.
